claims.claim_vi: A hotspot payment account is an account with a large number of concurrent operations; big accounts often cause hotspot issues in payment systems.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: When a merchant runs a promotion on a big sale day it receives many concurrent purchase orders and its account row in the database is updated frequently; normally a row lock is placed on the balance when it is updated, which gives low throughput and becomes a bottleneck.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Rate limiting restricts the number of requests in a period, the rest are rejected or retried later; it improves responsiveness for some users but can give a bad user experience.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Splitting the balance account into sub-accounts means one update request locks only one sub-account and the rest stay available.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Using a cache to update the balance first, with detailed statements and balances updated in the database later and asynchronously; the in-memory cache can handle much higher throughput than the database.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Costs of the sub-account and cache-first options (summing sub-accounts to read a total, one sub-account running dry while others have funds, losing a cached update if the cache fails before the database write) are the author's general knowledge.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against a database's or a payment system's documentation.

design_notes_vi: Khung một là ba bước nối nhau dẫn tới điểm nghẽn; khung hai là ba cách gỡ đặt cạnh nhau vì chúng là các lựa chọn, không phải một chuỗi.
source_deviations: The source gives the three optimizations as a list; the lesson adds, as marked general knowledge, what each one costs, which the source mentions only for rate limiting.
The source names large companies as examples; the lesson speaks of "a merchant" and "a big sale day" and names none.
The lesson does not say which option a real payment system uses.
